clue.text: Seems there has been a wrongful or conviction!

definitions.text: Seems there has been a wrongful or conviction!

parts.words: Seems there has been a wrongful or conviction!
parts.note: a court hearing followed by a mistaken guilty verdict reads as a hearing plus a blunder, which is also the name of learning by repeated attempts

explanation.surface: Someone suspects a miscarriage of justice has occurred.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR text has a stray 'or'; the reading is a court case that ends in a mistake, punning on the phrase for learning by repeated attempts.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the method of finding a solution by repeated attempts and learning from each mistake.

clue.text: Turned up in Paris — just for a snub!

definitions.text: Turned up in Paris — just for a snub!

parts.words: Turned up in Paris — just for a snub!
parts.note: the French word for 'turned up' is the term used in English for a snub, upturned nose

explanation.surface: Someone arrived in the French capital only to be cold-shouldered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' looks like 'arrived' and 'snub' like a rebuff; really it is a French adjective describing a snub nose.
explanation.definitionFit: The French adjective literally means turned up and describes a short, upward-tilted nose.

clue.text: Quite an affair and not too creditable?

definitions.text: Quite an affair and not too creditable?

parts.words: Quite an affair and not too creditable?
parts.note: a love affair, often an illicit one, is the French-derived word for a romance that does little credit to those in it

explanation.surface: Something was a big event and slightly disreputable.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a borrowed French term for a love affair, especially a secret or illicit one.

clue.text: Whence maybe low sounds in the

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Whence maybe low sounds in the (8)': cut short after 'the' (presumably a word like 'Channel'), so the cryptic reading about lowing cattle is incomplete.
annotationWithheld.clue: Whence maybe low sounds in the

clue.text: Hang over? Lag end of it anyhow.

definitions.text: Hang over?

indicators.note: anyhow means in any haphazard fashion, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

parts.words: Lag end

explanation.surface: A hungover person wonders what to do with the tail end of a drinking session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' jumbles the letters of LAG END; 'of it' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To dangle is to hang loosely or be suspended over something.

clue.text: Too much 'here, and turned all about.

definitions.text: Too much

indicators.note: all about means scattered around in every direction, so the letters of the two words are mixed up

parts.words: and turned

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they have had too much and their head is spinning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all about' rearranges AND TURNED; 'here' in the held text reads as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something superfluous is more than is needed, i.e. excessive.

clue.text: Are they seen when' printers are at daggers drawn?

definitions.text: Are they seen when' printers are at daggers drawn?

parts.words: Are they seen when' printers are at daggers drawn?
parts.note: printers' daggers are the reference marks used in typesetting; 'at daggers drawn' pretends to mean feuding

explanation.surface: A question about what appears when printers are quarrelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At daggers drawn' means bitterly hostile, but here printers literally draw daggers, the typographic marks of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the dagger-shaped marks printers use for footnote references or to flag doubtful passages.

clue.text: As a position it's inferior.

definitions.text: As a position it's inferior.

parts.words: As a position it's inferior.
parts.note: a state of being lower in rank is literally a position that is beneath others

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a job as a lowly one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes the condition of being lower in rank or under another's authority.

clue.text: Ascot gin toper, just the sort to give tips!

definitions.text: give tips

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange into order, so the letters of the racegoing phrase are reordered

parts.words: Ascot gin toper

explanation.surface: A hard-drinking racegoer at Ascot is just the type to pass on racing tips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort' looks like a noun meaning type but works as a verb, rearranging ASCOT GIN TOPER; 'just the' and 'to' are links. ASCOT is a famous English racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: To forecast what will happen is what a tipster does when offering predictions.

clue.text: Such were the ways of Wordsworth's

definitions.text: Such were the ways of Wordsworth's

parts.words: Such were the ways of Wordsworth's
parts.note: alludes to Wordsworth's Lucy poem beginning 'She dwelt among the ... ways', where the missing word describes paths nobody has walked

explanation.surface: A comment on the habits of the poet Wordsworth.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Wordsworth's 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways', about Lucy; 'ways' means paths, not habits.
explanation.definitionFit: Paths no one has walked on are unvisited and unworn.

clue.text: Medical man with an organ, very gloomy.

definitions.text: very gloomy

parts.words: Medical man
parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor, a medical man

parts.words: an organ
parts.note: the ear is an organ of hearing

explanation.surface: A doctor with a bodily complaint is in a very low mood.
explanation.definitionFit: The poetic adjective means dismal and cheerless, a shortened form of dreary.

clue.text: Nothing grim in this type of repute.

definitions.text: repute

parts.words: Nothing
parts.note: O is the digit zero, meaning nothing

parts.words: grim
parts.note: dour means stern and grim

explanation.surface: Nothing harsh is found in this kind of reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: The sense of 'repute' is that of being 'in good (or bad) odour' with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in good or bad odour with someone is to stand in good or bad esteem, i.e. reputation.

clue.text: In one sense a pitiful outcome.

definitions.text: In one sense a pitiful outcome.

parts.words: In one sense a pitiful outcome.
parts.note: 'pitiful' read as 'full of pity' rather than 'pathetic': softening towards someone is a compassionate result

explanation.surface: A sad result seems pathetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pitiful' usually means wretched, but here means showing pity: a person who softens and relents.
explanation.definitionFit: Becoming less severe and giving way out of compassion is the act described.

clue.text: A.B. knocked out for a while?

definitions.text: A.B. knocked out for a while?

parts.words: A.B. knocked out for a while?
parts.note: an able seaman put out of action has had his ability temporarily taken away

explanation.surface: A sailor has been punched unconscious for a time.
explanation.walkthrough: A.B. is the abbreviation for an able seaman; an able man knocked out is one made, for the moment, incapable.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone incapacitated, unable to function for the time being, is put out of action.

clue.text: Projectile in a snowball is ticklish to handle.

definitions.text: Projectile

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the following words of the clue

parts.words: snowball is ticklish

explanation.surface: A thrown snowball is a tricky thing to deal with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points into SNOWBALL IS TICKLISH; 'to handle' is a link. 'Projectile' is used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to missiles and their flight through the air.

clue.text: "The isles of Greece! Where loved and sung." (Byron.)

definitions.text: "The isles of Greece! Where loved and sung." (Byron.)

parts.words: "The isles of Greece! Where loved and sung." (Byron.)
parts.note: a gap-fill: Byron's line runs 'Where burning ... loved and sung', the missing name being the poet of Lesbos

explanation.surface: A quotation from Byron's poem about the Greek islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Byron's Don Juan: 'The isles of Greece! where burning Sappho loved and sung'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek lyric poet of Lesbos is the person celebrated in the line.

clue.text: You need to get inside here to understand properly.

definitions.text: You need to get inside here to understand properly.

parts.words: You need to get inside here to understand properly.
parts.note: the verb means both to get inside physically and to grasp a meaning fully

explanation.surface: Advice that you must look closely at something to grasp it.
explanation.definitionFit: To pierce into something and to fathom it are both senses of the verb.

clue.text: One of those safe chambers for a fellow lawyer?

definitions.text: One of those safe chambers for a fellow lawyer?

parts.words: One of those safe chambers for a fellow lawyer?
parts.note: a fortified gun chamber, read jokingly as a colleague on a legal case

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a secure office suits a barrister's colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chambers' suggests barristers' offices, but the answer is a bombproof chamber in a fortress or warship.
explanation.definitionFit: A vaulted, armoured chamber in a fortification or ship, from which guns are fired.

clue.text: "Man for, the sword and' for (Tennyson.).

definitions.text: "Man for, the sword and' for (Tennyson.).

parts.words: "Man for, the sword and' for (Tennyson.).
parts.note: a gap-fill from Tennyson's The Princess: 'Man for the sword and for the ... she', the missing word being a sewing tool

explanation.surface: A quotation from Tennyson on the roles of men and women.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's line is 'Man for the sword and for the needle she'; the held text is garbled by OCR but the gap is plain.
explanation.definitionFit: The sewing implement is set against the sword in the line as woman's work.

clue.text: One of a pair that clicks

definitions.text: One of a pair that clicks

parts.words: One of a pair that clicks
parts.note: a couple who get on well 'click', but here it is a handheld percussion instrument used in pairs

explanation.surface: One member of a couple who get on well together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clicks' suggests rapport between two people; the answer is a Spanish percussion shell.
explanation.definitionFit: The percussion instrument consists of two wooden shells clicked together in the hand.

clue.text: It can't be said this doesn't come off for want 'of a better

definitions.text: It can't be said this doesn't come off for want 'of a better

parts.words: It can't be said this doesn't come off for want 'of a better
parts.note: a risky bet does not 'come off' for lack of a better one: a wager that fails is still this

explanation.surface: Something fails only because nothing better was available.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'come off' means to succeed; a speculation sometimes does and sometimes doesn't.
explanation.definitionFit: A wager or risky venture may or may not succeed.

clue.text: This finish — it's one way to attire men.

definitions.text: finish

indicators.note: one way to arrange signals that these letters are put in another order

parts.words: attire men

explanation.surface: Dressing the men is one way of ending things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one way to' signals a rearrangement of ATTIRE MEN; 'This' and 'it's' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring something to an end is to conclude it.

clue.text: A help possibly to a sense of proportion.

definitions.text: A help possibly to a sense of proportion.

parts.words: A help possibly to a sense of proportion.
parts.note: a sense of proportion suggests good judgement, but here it is the mathematical relation of quantities

explanation.surface: Something might help someone keep things in perspective.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sense of proportion' sounds like sound judgement; the answer is the quantitative relation between two amounts.
explanation.definitionFit: A proportion between two quantities is expressed as this relation.

clue.text: Alien, the staying sort.

definitions.text: Alien, the staying sort.

parts.words: Alien, the staying sort.
parts.note: a foreigner who settled and lived in an ancient Greek city with some civic rights

explanation.surface: A foreigner who has come to stay.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Athens a resident foreigner with limited citizen rights was given this name.

clue.text: Mohammedan legal. expert in plain clothes too.

definitions.text: Mohammedan legal. expert
definitions.meaning: an Islamic scholar who gives rulings on religious law

definitions.text: plain clothes
definitions.meaning: civilian dress worn by someone usually in uniform

explanation.surface: An Islamic jurist is dressed in civilian clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a Muslim jurist and the civvies an off-duty serviceman wears.

clue.text: Some musicians, perhaps, turning tween seven and nine.

definitions.text: Some musicians, perhaps, turning tween seven and nine.

parts.words: Some musicians, perhaps, turning tween seven and nine.
parts.note: the number between seven and nine gives a group of eight players

explanation.surface: Some musicians are performing in the evening between seven and nine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seven and nine' looks like clock times; the number between them gives the group size.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of eight performers, or a piece for them.

clue.text: Jollification — fatal for the pulse!

definitions.text: Jollification
fatal for the pulse!
definitions.meaning: a pulse is a pea or bean, and a feast on them is the end for that vegetable

explanation.surface: A party proves deadly for someone's heartbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulse' looks like a heartbeat but means a legume.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowdy party or outing, literally a feast on legumes.

clue.text: It may well confuse the basis of housing.

definitions.text: It may well confuse the basis of housing.

parts.words: It may well confuse the basis of housing.
parts.note: 'confuse' in its literal sense of pouring together: a machine that blends cement, sand and gravel for foundations

explanation.surface: Something might muddle the fundamentals of housing policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confuse' literally means to mix together, which is what the rotating drum does to building material.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating drum machine mixes cement, aggregate and water for building foundations.
